name: One-line beats that earn their isolation
instruction: This story may set short lines or single sentences off on their own. Judge whether those isolations do dramatic work IN CONTEXT: an isolated line should land a turn, a reveal, a shift of attention, or a beat of silence that the surrounding prose has set up, and the story should return to ordinary paragraphing when nothing is being marked. Score 1.0 when nearly every isolated line is placed where a beat belongs and the effect would be lost if it were folded back into the preceding paragraph. Score 0.5 when some isolations do work and others are arbitrary. Score 0.0 when lines are isolated indiscriminately or habitually, so the breaks mark nothing in particular, AND also 0.0 when the story isolates nothing but plainly needed a beat somewhere. Answer NA only if the story is too short to show any paragraphing pattern. Judge the placement, not the quantity: a story with three well-placed breaks scores higher than one with thirty indiscriminate ones.
rationale: Isolates the candidate-REAL component: deliberate one-line beats serving tension and pacing, judged in context. Explicitly decouples from density (three well-placed breaks beat thirty indiscriminate ones) so it can score high where the surface component scores low and vice versa.

name: Blank-line and short-paragraph density
instruction: Count the typographic density of the story's paragraphing: what fraction of its paragraphs are a single short clause or sentence set off by its own line break, and how much blank vertical space the text uses overall. Score 1.0 when most paragraphs are one-line beats and the text is visually very airy; 0.5 when there is a moderate mix; 0.0 when the story is built from ordinary multi-sentence paragraphs with little blank space. Count the formatting only. Pay no attention to whether any break is well placed, whether it marks anything, or whether the story reads better or worse for it.
rationale: Isolates the SURFACE component: the blank-line / paste-formatting habit alone, counted with no judgement of effect. This is the component the two retired parent channels were actually measuring.

name: Revision depth: continuity, economy, and closed setups
instruction:
Read the writing prompt and the story, then judge how much substantive reworking the text shows in its CONTENT. Assess four things:
(a) Continuity -- do established facts hold? Character names, ages, relationships, physical details, locations, the timeline, and who knows what at each point should stay consistent, with no drift or contradiction.
(b) Economy -- is each paragraph doing work? Look for redundant sentences, beats restated in different words, throat-clearing before the story starts, and passages that could be cut with no loss.
(c) Closure of setups -- are objects, details, and promises introduced early actually used, paid off, or deliberately left open, rather than simply dropped and forgotten?
(d) Control of tense and point of view -- is the narrating stance held deliberately, with any shift reading as a choice, rather than as the writer losing track mid-scene?
HIGH = the story reads as if it has been gone over: nothing contradicts itself, little could be cut, what is planted is used, the narrating stance is under control.
LOW = the story reads as a single unrevised pass: internal details drift or contradict, passages repeat or wander, elements are introduced and abandoned, the narrating stance slips without purpose.
EXPLICITLY IGNORE all spelling, punctuation, capitalization, apostrophes, paragraph spacing, and formatting. A story riddled with typos can and should score HIGH here if the four properties above hold; a mechanically flawless story can and should score LOW if they do not. Do not reward ambition, subject matter, genre, length, or prose flourish; judge only (a)-(d). Use only the prompt and the story -- do not speculate about the writer, and do not consider how the story was received.
rationale: Isolates what revision does TO a story from what it leaves ON it. Each listed property requires reading for meaning and holding the whole text in mind: none is detectable by a spellchecker, and none is conferred on a writer who merely ran one. The explicit order to ignore all orthography strips the fingerprint out, so the score cannot ride on mechanical cleanliness. What is left is something a careful editor would call quality on its own terms -- a story whose facts hold, whose setups pay, and which has nothing spare is better reading whether or not anyone ever edited it. The two components come apart in both directions: spellchecked-but-unrevised prose (including machine-drafted text) scores clean-and-shallow, while a hastily typed story by a dyslexic or non-native writer who reworked its structure scores messy-and-deep.

name: Mechanical slip count (spellchecker-catchable surface errors)
instruction:
Tally mechanical surface errors only. Make no judgement about whether they help or hurt the story. Count visible instances of: misspellings and typos; transposed, dropped, or doubled letters; homophone confusions (their/there, its/it's, your/you're); dropped or doubled words; subject-verb agreement errors; missing, doubled, or misplaced apostrophes; unclosed or mismatched quotation marks; inconsistent capitalization of the same word; inconsistent paragraph spacing or indentation; inconsistent typographic conventions (straight and curly quotes mixed, a hyphen used where a dash is used elsewhere, ellipses spelled inconsistently); and the same proper name spelled two different ways.
HIGH = many such instances are visible, judged relative to the length of the text.
LOW = the text is mechanically clean, with essentially none.
Do NOT count as errors: sustained deliberate stylistic choices, such as dialect or eye-dialect spellings, an unpunctuated or all-lowercase style, or fragments used throughout -- if a convention is applied consistently across the text it is a style, not a slip. Do NOT count tense shifts, point-of-view shifts, plot contradictions, repetition, or anything requiring you to track the story's content. Do not consider whether the story is good, coherent, interesting, or well structured; read only closely enough to spot the slips. Use only the prompt and the story -- do not speculate about the writer, and do not consider how the story was received.
rationale: Pure trace. Every counted item is something a spellchecker, a grammar tool, or one proofreading pass removes without changing a single thing about the story, so the score is a fingerprint of tool access and proofing labour rather than of the writing itself. Framing it as a tally, with an explicit ban on judging whether the slips hurt, keeps evaluative judgement out. Excluding sustained stylistic choices stops the criterion from punishing deliberate voice, which would smuggle craft judgement back in; excluding tense, POV, and contradiction stops it from double-scoring the real component. The contested boundary is naming, which three of the five parent channels leave ambiguous: mere orthographic variants of a name are counted here, while drift in a character's established details belongs to the candidate-real component.
